doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Record companies and European royalties
summary: Record companies avoid royalties, while European societies enforce them and respect composers.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Have you had good or bad luck dealing with record companies over the years?

Well in a way you can look at it two ways. It was good that you got to record as far as the popularity is concerned. But record companies have a very strange business ethic. Very strange. And it isn’t good for the artist. And I haven’t understood yet what it is that they’re trying to achieve. It looks like they’re mainly building up a catalogue and then selling it. That seems to be what they’re — they never seem to try to keep the record company building in a way that it’s going to last. Because for some reason they don’t really believe in paying royalties see. But now in Europe they pay royalties. See they’ve got some organizations over there like Cessane in Germany, GAMA, you have to pay royalties over there. If somebody whistles your music on the street they’ve got to pay. If a band plays your song — a marching band — they have to pay. And in the clubs if you play and you don’t put all the music down they’ll say well we were there on Thursday night and you played Thelonious Monk and you don’t have it on here.
These are representatives of those organizations?
Yeah. They have a great respect for composers because they had all those great composers in the classical music over there so that developed from that time.
